answer: The two methods combine learned representations at different levels and for different purposes. node2vec combines the embeddings of two nodes into a single edge representation using simple binary operators: average, Hadamard (element-wise product), weighted L1 distance, and weighted L2 distance. These are meant to build edge features for link prediction, so the Hadamard product captures pairwise feature interactions, while the L1/L2 operators capture difference or distance between the endpoints. LINE instead combines representations at the node level. It trains first-order proximity embeddings (for direct, observed ties) and second-order proximity embeddings (for nodes sharing neighbourhood context) separately, then concatenates them into one vector per node. The concatenation is meant to preserve both local and higher-order structural proximity in a single node representation, without fusing the two signals into a shared space. In short, node2vec's combinations represent the relationship between a pair of nodes (edges), while LINE's combination represents a single node's multi-scale neighbourhood structure.
